title: In re BROWN, WALTER R., BIIA Dec., 41,766 (1974)
text:
Brown, Walter
CUSTODY OF CHILDREN
Determined by court order
A court order granting the worker's wife custody of their children during the pendency of
a divorce action determines the custody of the children for purposes of RCW 51.32.010.
The wife, not the worker, was therefore entitled to back pension payments on the
children's account during a reconciliation period when the worker returned to live with
the wife and children. ….In re Walter Brown, BIIA Dec., 41,766 (1974)
Scroll down for order.

BEFORE THE BOARD OF INDUSTRIAL INSURANCE APPEALS
STATE OF WASHINGTON
1
IN RE: WALTER R. BROWN ) DOCKET NO. 41,766
2
)
3
CLAIM NO. F569258 ) DECISION AND ORDER
4
5
APPEARANCES:
6
7 Claimant, Walter R. Brown, by
8 Combs, Small & Kucklick, per
9 Alfred J. Kucklick
10
11 Employer, Zidell Dismantling, Inc.,
12 None
13
14 Department of Labor and Industries, by
15 The Attorney General, per
16 Gary Rentel, Assistant
17
18 This is an appeal filed by the claimant on November 16, 1972, from an order of the
19
Department of Labor and Industries dated November 2, 1972 which adhered to a prior Department
20
21 determination concerning division of back pension payments, for the period from December 26,
22
1969 to September 15, 1971, between the claimant herein and his divorced spouse as custodian of
23
24 their minor children. REVERSED AND REMANDED, IN PART.
25
DECISION
26
27 Pursuant to RCW 51.52.104 and RCW 51.52.106, this matter is before the Board for review
28
and decision on a timely Petition for Review filed by the Department of Labor and Industries (and
29
30 claimant's answer thereto) to a Proposed Decision and Order issued by a hearing examiner for this
31
Board on July 13, 1973, in which the order of the Department dated November 2, 1972 was
32
33 reversed, and the matter remanded to the Department with instruction to recompute moneys due
34
the claimant herein on the basis that for the period from December 26, 1969 to April 20, 1971, the
35
36 claimant was entitled to the entire amount of back pension payments, including the portion thereof
37
payable on account of his children.
38
39 At issue before us, on the Department's Petition for Review, is a sum of retroactive pension
40
payments allowable to the claimant's five minor children, covering the period from December 26,
41
42 1969 to April 20, 1971 in regard to four of the children, and from February 23, 1970 to April 20,
43
1971 in regard to one child-- the question being whether the Department was correct in paying
44
45 these accrued children's benefits to the claimant's ex-wife on behalf of the children, or whether such
46
benefits should have been paid directly to the claimant.
47
1
7/15/74

1
The pertinent facts are as follows:
2
On September 16, 1968, the claimant's then wife filed suit for a divorce from the claimant in
3
4
Pierce County Superior Court. At that time they had been separated for a couple of months. On
5
October 25, 1968, the Court entered an order awarding the wife custody of the couple's four minor
6
7
children. On or about October 15, 1969, the claimant moved back home with his wife and four
8
children. A fifth child was born on February 23, 1970, having been conceived between the parties
9
10
in May 1969. On December 1, 1970, the wife filed an amended complaint for divorce, and on that
11
same date the claimant again moved out of the home. On April 20, 1971, the claimant's wife was
12
13
granted a final decree of divorce, wherein she was awarded permanent custody of all five minor
14
children.
15
16
While the claimant's claim for his industrial injury of July 10, 1967 was open for treatment, he
17
was directly paid time loss compensation at the full statutory rate of $329.00 per month, from
18
19
October 26, 1968 to April 11, 1969. Evidently, on or about the latter date the Department learned of
20
the 1968 custody award by the Court of the children to the claimant's then wife. Thus, from April
21
22
11, 1969 to December 26, 1969 (when the Department terminated time loss compensation, the
23
claimant's time loss payments sent directly to him were reduced by $114.00 per month (portion
24
25
allocable to the four children) and this amount was in turn paid monthly by the Department into the
26
Pierce County Superior Court, for the benefit of said children.
27
28
Following the Department's closure of the claim with a permanent partial disability award,
29
and an appeal therefrom to this Board, a final Board decision was entered on August 20, 1971,
30
31
which found the claimant to be permanently and totally disabled as of December 26, 1969, and
32
ordered payment of a pension commencing as of that date. Accordingly, by order dated September
33
34
2, 1971, the Department placed the claimant on the pension rolls effective December 26, 1969, and
35
thereafter paid the claimant a lump-sum award for back pension payments accrued for the period
36
37
from December 26, 1969 to September 15, 1971, less the children's portion of such payments. The
38
Department paid the children's portion in a lump sum to the claimant's ex-wife, pursuant to the
39
40
proviso of RCW 51.32.010, prescribing:
41
"That, if an injured workman, or the surviving spouse of an injured
42
workman shall not have the custody of a child for, or on account of
43
whom payments are required to be made under this chapter, such
44
payment or payments shall be made to the person having the lawful
45
custody of such child."
46
47
2

1
It was from the Department's subsequent order, affirming this apportionment of the retroactive
2
pension payments, that the instant appeal was filed.
3
4
At the hearing stage of these proceedings, it was the claimant's contention that he, instead of
5
his ex-wife, was entitled to receive the children's portion of his back pension payments for the
6
7
period covering December 26, 1969 to December 1, 1970, since he had moved back home prior to
8
December 26, 1969 and continued to reside at home until December 1, 1970, at which time his wife
9
10
filed the amended divorce complaint and he again moved out. Thus, so the claimant contended, he
11
had custody of his children during that period. The hearing examiner however, went a step further
12
13
and proposed to grant the children's portion of the back pension payments to the claimant for the
14
entire period from December 26, 1969 to April 20, 1971. On petition for review before the Board by
15
16
the Department, the claimant, quite naturally, in a reply to the Department's petition, urges the
17
adoption of the hearing examiner's disposition in toto.
18
19
Unfortunately, the hearing examiner did not completely spell out the basis for his decision,
20
except to note the last phrase of the above-quoted proviso of RCW 51.32.010, speaking of lawful
21
22
custody of such child." Presumably, it was his interpretation of this phrase that so long as the
23
thread of a legal marriage existed between the parties, the claimant, as the father, must be deemed
24
25
to have custody of his children as a matter of law, and that only the final divorce decree of April 20,
26
1971, awarding permanent custody to the mother, could be said to have changed this result. We
27
28
do not agree.
29
As previously noted, custody of the children was initially awarded to the mother by an order
30
31
of the Court dated October 25, 1968. In other words, responsibility for the care, keeping, and
32
control of the four children then existing was legally vested in the mother. Obviously the Court then
33
34
felt this was in the children's best interests--which, after all, is the overriding primary concern in
35
these matters. No subsequent order of the Court was entered--either in the pending divorce action
36
37
itself, or in regard to custody of the children--until April 20, 1971, when a final decree of divorce was
38
granted to the wife, along with permanent custody of all five children. The claimant, however, takes
39
40
the position that the continuity of custody was broken upon his return to the home in October 1969,
41
in that such return vitiated the divorce proceeding and the ancillary custody order of October 25,
42
43
1968, citing McFerran v. McFerran, 47 Wn. 2d 236, and the earlier case cited therein of Yoder v.
44
Yoder, 105 Wash. 491, for the proposition that "reconciliation incontestably terminates the divorce
45
46
action".
47
3

1
Quite obviously, the claimant's theory of the case pre-supposes that his return to board and
2
bed in October 1969 constituted a "reconciliation." Maybe it did, and then again, maybe it did not.
3
4
Or maybe a reconciliation occurred in May 1969, when the fifth child was conceived. Most
5
certainly, there was a return by the claimant--if not to board, at least to bed--at that time also.
6
7
However, the important point is: it is not for this tribunal to say either when or if a divorce
8
proceeding pending before a superior court of this state was terminated. We have no quarrel with
9
10
the general proposition that reconciliation terminates a divorce action. Nor do we question for a
11
moment the claimant's right to have had the pending divorce action against him in Superior Court
12
13
dismissed, had the matter of a true reconciliation been brought to the Court's attention and been
14
judicially established. The McFerran case, supra, recognizes the propriety of such a procedure.
15
16
The fact of the matter is, however, that this was not the case here. The divorce proceeding was
17
never dismissed nor terminated, but continued in force (along with the custody order of October 25,
18
19
1968) from its initial filing, on September 16, 1968, to the entry of a final decree on April 20, 1971.
20
The only intervening factor was the filing of an amended complaint in the original divorce action on
21
22
December 1, 1970. The amended complaint was entitled "Cause No. 184630", the same cause
23
number as the original complaint. In short, there was but one divorce action. If in fact the parties
24
25
became reconciled during the pendency of the divorce action, the absence of judicial notarization of
26
such reconciliation through a dismissal of the divorce action precludes its recognition by this Board.
27
28
To do otherwise would, in effect, permit a lawful and standing order of the Court to be collaterally
29
assaulted and avoided by the claimant through proceedings before the Board. It is a basic tenet of
30
31
the law that absent fraud, a duly entered order of the court can only be vacated or overturned in the
32
same proceeding and is not subject to collateral attack by a party thereto in a different proceeding.
33
34
In summary, we hold that during the period from December 26, 1969 to April 20, 1971, the
35
general welfare and custody of the claimant's first four minor children were matters under the
36
37
authority and jurisdiction of the Superior Court for Pierce County, and that Court's order of October
38
25, 1968, awarding custody to their mother, was in continuous force and effect, so that the
39
40
Department had no alternative but to pay such children's portion of the claimant's retroactive
41
pension payments covering the afore-stated time period to the mother for the benefit of the children,
42
43
under the mandate of the proviso in RCW 51.32.010.
44
As for the couple's fifth child, born on February 23, 1970, a different result necessarily
45
46
obtains. The Court's custody order of October 25, 1968 did not, of course, encompass this after
47
4

1
born child. There was no order of the Court governing its custody or otherwise affecting its status
2
until the final divorce decree was entered on April 20, 1971, at which time the custody of the fifth
3
4
child was awarded to the mother, along with the other four children. Thus, for the period prior to
5
April 20, 1971, the divorce action in court cannot be controlling as to "custody" of this child. Rather,
6
7
since the facts are that the claimant fathered said child and resided in the home with said child from
8
the time of its birth on February 23, 1970 to the time the claimant left the home on December 1,
9
10
1970, we think it must be held that he did have actual custody as to this one child for that particular
11
period of time, and is therefore the proper recipient of the compensation payable for such period on
12
13
account of the fifth child.
14
The factual matters in this case were not disputed by the parties, and have heretofore been
15
16
fully recited. Accordingly, formal findings of fact need not be entered. RCW 51.52.106.
17
In accordance with our decision herein, the order of the Department of Labor and Industries
18
19
dated November 2, 1972, must be, and hereby is, reversed, solely to the extent that the claim is
20
remanded to the Department with instructions to pay the claimant that portion of the pension
21
22
allocable to his fifth child, for the period from February 23, 1970 to December 1, 1970. In all other
23
respects, the Department's order of November 2, 1972 is hereby sustained.
24
25
It is so ORDERED.
26
27
Dated this 15th day of July, 1974.
